Section B: Impact of thermal expansion on junction conductance Thermal expansion of a NPoM junction is considered by performing COMSOL simulations of the full NPoM device (Figure S6). The device is modelled according to the multilayer structure described in the main text, including a constant power heat source to simulate optical heating from the laser (up to 0.1mW used in experiments) and then allowing the system to reach thermal equilibrium. Results show that at maximum power the temperature gradient across the junction gap is <5K, largely independent of whether the heating source is applied to the AuNP or the gap itself. The mechanical response is dominated by PMMA expansion, that lifts up the NP and generates a positive strain on the SAM (<1% at maximum power, Figure S6b). Through the exponential conductance vs gap size dependence in Figure 1e (main text) this would translate into a drop in conductance of up to 3% at maximum power (Figure S6c).

Figure S6. Thermal expansion. a, COMSOL model of heating in the junction, with stationary temperature map at 0.1mW heating power applied across the tunnelling gap. b, PMMA expansion results in positive strain (increase in gap size) upon heating. c, Modulus of thermally induced conductance change resulting from gap strain. Experimentally, we measure the I-V response of a 6Cdt junction at low bias (≤0.1V) over 10 full sweeps while toggling laser illumination ON/OFF after each +V/-V sweep, and plot in Figure S7 the average of each set of sweeps. The traces for laser ON/OFF overlap within experimental uncertainty. The dashed line in Figure S7 is the calculated -3% conductance change from the laser OFF trace, to compare with


<!-- Page 4 -->


the simulation prediction at full laser power. This calculated trace is on the edge of experimental uncertainty, but clearly distinguishable from the experimental ‘laser ON’ trace. Therefore we conclude that photothermal change in gap conductance is a very weak effect, with negligible impact on our results. This can be expected since 0.1mW heating power significantly overestimates the actual heating delivered by the laser. The top Au electrode reflects >60% of incoming radiation, and the NP diameter is a tenth of the laser spot size, so the net optical power reaching the NP is of the order of 10-4-10-

3mW, causing negligible thermally induced strain in the junction gap.

Figure S7. Low bias conductance with illumination. Laser irradiation does not change junction conductance and no thermal expansion of the gap is observed experimentally.
